claim: Most human gastric cancer worldwide is ascribed to Helicobacter pylori infections.
source: Most of the human gastric cancer (GC) worldwide are ascribed to Helicobacter pylori infections, which have a detrimental effect on the immunotherapy's efficacy.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established scientific understanding about the relationship between H. pylori and gastric cancer.

claim: H. pylori infections have a detrimental effect on immunotherapy's efficacy.
source: Most of the human gastric cancer (GC) worldwide are ascribed to Helicobacter pylori infections, which have a detrimental effect on the immunotherapy's efficacy.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the manuscript and is a key premise of the study.

claim: The study performed comprehensive single-cell transcriptome analysis of nine GC patients with current H. pylori infection (HpGC), three GC patients with previous H. pylori infection (ex-HpGC), six GC patients without H. pylori infection (non-HpGC), and six healthy controls (HC).
source: We performed a comprehensive single-cell transcriptome analysis of nine GC patients with current H. pylori infection (HpGC), three GC patients with previous H. pylori infection (ex-HpGC), six GC patients without H. pylori infection (non-HpGC), and six healthy controls (HC).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample composition of the study.

claim: The malignant epithelium of HpGC exhibited high expression level of inflammatory and epithelial–mesenchymal transition signature.
source: The malignant epithelium of HpGC exhibited high expression level of inflammatory and epithelial–mesenchymal transition signature
evidence: This finding is supported by the scRNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: HpGC and ex-HpGC were enriched with VEGFA+ angiogenic tumor-associated macrophages (Angio-TAM) and IL11+ inflammatory CAF (iCAF).
source: HpGC and ex-HpGC were enriched with VEGFA+ angiogenic tumor-associated macrophages (Angio-TAM) and IL11+ inflammatory CAF (iCAF), characterized by high expression levels of NECTIN2 and VEGFA/B.
evidence: This is a key finding from the single-cell analysis presented in the results.

claim: Angio-TAM and iCAF are characterized by high expression levels of NECTIN2 and VEGFA/B.
source: HpGC and ex-HpGC were enriched with VEGFA+ angiogenic tumor-associated macrophages (Angio-TAM) and IL11+ inflammatory CAF (iCAF), characterized by high expression levels of NECTIN2 and VEGFA/B.
evidence: This molecular characterization is derived from gene expression analysis in the study.

claim: There are significant correlations between the abundance of iCAF with Angio-TAM and TIGIT+ suppressive T cells.
source: Additionally, we found significant correlations between the abundance of iCAF with Angio-TAM and TIGIT+ suppressive T cells
evidence: This correlation analysis is presented in the results section of the manuscript.

claim: iCAF interacted with Angio-TAM through the VEGF and ANGPTL angiogenic pathways.
source: iCAF interacted with Angio-TAM through the VEGF and ANGPTL angiogenic pathways.
evidence: This interaction is identified through intercellular crosstalk analysis in the study.

claim: The iCAF abundance and angiogenic signature could predict poor immunotherapy outcomes in GC.
source: We also developed an immune signature and angiogenic signature and demonstrated that the iCAF abundance and angiogenic signature could predict poor immunotherapy outcomes in GC.
evidence: This predictive capability is demonstrated through analysis of immunotherapy response data.

claim: Gastric cancer is the fifth most diagnosed tumor and the third most common cause of cancer-causing death.
source: Gastric cancer (GC) is the fifth most diagnosed tumor and the third most common cause of cancer-causing death.
evidence: This is a statement of epidemiological fact from established cancer statistics.

claim: H. pylori infection is responsible for approximately 90% of noncardia GC worldwide.
source: Helicobacter pylori infection (Uemura et al., 2001; Hsu et al., 2007) is an important carcinogenic factor and responsible for approximately 90% of noncardia GC worldwide and approximately 5% of the total burden from all cancers globally (Plummer et al., 2015).
evidence: This statistic is cited from published literature (Plummer et al., 2015).

claim: H. pylori infection is responsible for approximately 5% of the total burden from all cancers globally.
source: Helicobacter pylori infection (Uemura et al., 2001; Hsu et al., 2007) is an important carcinogenic factor and responsible for approximately 90% of noncardia GC worldwide and approximately 5% of the total burden from all cancers globally (Plummer et al., 2015).
evidence: This global cancer burden statistic is cited from Plummer et al., 2015.

claim: H. pylori infection plays a critical role in TME regulation and is linked to response to immunotherapies.
source: It also plays a critical role in TME regulation and is linked to response to immunotherapies (Oster et al., 2022; Hatakeyama, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Oster et al., 2022 and Hatakeyama, 2006.

claim: H. pylori infection status correlated with different molecular characteristics.
source: According to the histological examination, serology test, rapid urease test, and H. pylori DNA validation, H. pylori infection-associated GC cases can be classified into current H. pylori infection and past H. pylori infection, and the H. pylori infection status correlated with different molecular characteristics (Kwak et al., 2014; Son et al., 2022).
evidence: This correlation is cited from Kwak et al., 2014 and Son et al., 2022.

claim: The JAVELIN Gastric 300 study showed that PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors do not have significant advantages over conventional chemotherapy in the treatment of GC.
source: Previous clinical trial studies such as JAVELIN Gastric 300 (Bang et al., 2018), KEYNOTE-061 (Shitara et al., 2018), and KEYNOTE-062 (Shitara et al., 2020) have shown that PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors do not have significant advantages over conventional chemotherapy in the treatment of GC.
evidence: This clinical trial result is cited from Bang et al., 2018.

claim: The CheckMate-649 study revealed that the continued use of nivolumab plus chemotherapy as a standard first-line treatment achieved great success in advanced gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma.
source: In contrast, the CheckMate-649 study has revealed that the continued use of nivolumab plus chemotherapy as a standard first-line treatment achieved great success in advanced gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (Shitara et al., 2022).
evidence: This clinical trial result is cited from Shitara et al., 2022.

claim: The Asian population benefits more from immunotherapy than the global population.
source: A subgroup analysis has revealed that the Asian population benefits more from immunotherapy than the global population, and among the Asian population, the Chinese population benefits the most from immunotherapy, which could be ascribed to the molecular features leading to GC in Chinese patients, such as H. pylori infection (Zhang et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2020).
evidence: This subgroup analysis finding is cited from Zhang et al., 2022 and Peng et al., 2020.

claim: Among the Asian population, the Chinese population benefits the most from immunotherapy.
source: A subgroup analysis has revealed that the Asian population benefits more from immunotherapy than the global population, and among the Asian population, the Chinese population benefits the most from immunotherapy, which could be ascribed to the molecular features leading to GC in Chinese patients, such as H. pylori infection (Zhang et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2020).
evidence: This finding is cited from Zhang et al., 2022 and Peng et al., 2020.

claim: H. pylori infection hindered the efficacy of immune checkpoint-targeting PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors through immune evasion, T cell suppression, and fluctuation in the intestinal flora.
source: However, recent studies have demonstrated that H. pylori infection hindered the efficacy of immune checkpoint-targeting PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors or vaccine-based immunotherapies through immune evasion, T cell suppression, and fluctuation in the intestinal flora, compromising the benefits of cancer immunotherapies (Oster et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2022).
evidence: This mechanism is cited from Oster et al., 2022 and Shi et al., 2022.
